doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Ken Burns and his jazz series
summary: Crohn recalls being asked to lunch by Burns' office, and criticises the Bird clip cut and the reliance on Crouch and Marsalis.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: When you heard about — did you know about Ken Burns’ thing before it was aired?

Yes. They even came to me. Somebody from Ken Burns’ office called me up and said, “Let’s have lunch.” And I said ooh, maybe there’s something in it for me. And on the phone I said I’d love to — if you need someone to produce some segments I’d love to do it. “Oh no, we have people to do that.” They didn’t want it. They just wanted to pick my brain. They didn’t offer me anything.
Someone recommended our interviews too and it didn’t go anywhere.

Right. No Ken Burns, as someone said, Ken Burns gets all the money, which isn’t very nice, but he’s like this big boat. It’s like if you’re paddling someplace and this big tanker comes through, it upsets the little boats. He also takes all the money that might be reserved for us other little filmmakers, whatever money there is for jazz.
Right. What did you think of his jazz film?

I’m saying this on camera for posterity. It just had some problems with it. I think, if I remember correctly, he had a thing on Bird and there’s only one clip of Bird, at the time anyway, the Hothouse clip with Dizzy and all that. And there’s one thirty-two bar chorus of Bird on film. And he cuts it off after the bridge if I remember correctly. And I think I threw a shoe at the TV set. I might be wrong about that. I remember I think he did cut into it with narration, he cut it off. I mean you don’t cut in to a Bird solo when it’s the only one there is on film. And there are other things.
I know, me too, me too.
Also, he didn’t know anything about jazz when he started.
That’s what irked me to start with.

So he relied on Stanley Crouch and Wynton Marsalis, and, you know, God bless both of them, they’ve done a lot for jazz and I respect Stanley as a writer and I certainly respect Wynton, because I’ve worked with Wynton and he’s got an incredible mind. But he wasn’t immersed. It’s like, you know when you’re immersed in the music from the way up you would have made a different film than you would if you had just come to it new and have to learn it while you’re doing it.
